## Awanakancha in Peru: Llamas, Alpacas, and Traditional Andean Weaving

**Awanakancha is a cultural and textile center on the road from Cusco toward Pisac.** Visitors come to see South American camelids, learn about their fibers, and discover the crafts practiced by highland communities. Unlike the archaeological complexes of the Sacred Valley, the highlights here are living animals and artisans at work.

It is also a chance to understand where traditional Andean textiles come from, why different fibers have different values, and how patterns relate to the lives of local communities. A visit can be a short stop along the way or part of a fuller day devoted to culture.

## What Animals Can You See at Awanakancha?

The center features **llamas, alpacas, vicuñas, and guanacos**. All belong to the South American camelid family, but they differ in their lifestyles, appearance, and relationships with humans.

| Animal | What to Know |
|---|---|
| Llama | Traditionally used as a pack animal |
| Alpaca | Raised for its valuable fiber |
| Vicuña | Wild species with exceptionally fine fiber |
| Guanaco | Wild relative of the llama |

**Llamas** are larger animals historically used to carry loads in mountainous areas. **Alpacas** are best known for the fiber used to make soft textiles and clothing. **Vicuñas** inhabit high-altitude ecosystems and are renowned for their exceptionally fine fiber; as wild animals, their care and handling are regulated. **Guanacos** are also wild and should not be confused with domesticated llamas.

Observing the animals can interest both adults and children, but all interaction must follow staff instructions. Feeding opportunities and the species and number of animals on site should be confirmed for your visit rather than assumed to be constant.

## Why Is the Center Associated with Weaving?

Awanakancha introduces visitors to **the entire journey from fiber to finished fabric**. The official Perú Travel description mentions shearing, preparing and spinning fiber, producing dyes, and working at the loom. Special attention is given to artisans from Andean communities and preserving skills passed down through generations.

Watching this work becomes more meaningful when a guide explains each stage. First, the fiber is collected and prepared, then spun into yarn. Next, the threads are dyed and used to create textiles featuring characteristic colors and geometric patterns.

Different techniques and materials produce different results. The softness of a finished item depends not only on the animal named on its label but also on the quality of the fiber, its processing, the yarn, and the weave itself. That is why speaking with artisans about their methods can be more enlightening than comparing prices in a souvenir shop.

## Natural Dyes and Andean Patterns

Traditional dyeing may use plants, minerals, and other natural substances. Peru's official tourism portal describes demonstrations in which craftswomen explain where different shades come from and how threads are treated. Visitors can see the direct connection between materials found in nature and the colors of the resulting fabric.

The patterns themselves are equally interesting. In Andean textiles, motifs may relate to a particular place, a community's traditions, the type of garment, and generations of artisans. It would be misleading to assign one universal “ancient meaning” to every geometric symbol: meanings vary across regions and traditions.

If you are considering a purchase, ask who made the item, which fiber was used, and what technique produced it. Because the center introduces you to the craft before you shop, a souvenir can become a meaningful reminder of your visit.

## Where Is Awanakancha?

Awanakancha lies on the **Cusco–Pisac road**, toward the [Sacred Valley of the Incas](/peru/place/sacred-valley-of-the-incas/). Tour operators and tourism services place it near kilometer 23 of this road, making it convenient to include on a route to [Pisac](/peru/place/pisac/) or other sites in the valley.

A visit differs from a trip to [Moray](/peru/place/moray/), whose main attraction is its ancient circular agricultural terraces. It also differs from visiting [Ollantaytambo](/peru/place/ollantaytambo/), with its Inca buildings and historic infrastructure.

These nearby sites make it possible to plan a varied cultural day. Allow enough time for the craft demonstrations, however: a quick stop to photograph the animals reveals only part of what Awanakancha has to offer.

## Altitude, Weather, and Practical Preparation

The center is situated at an altitude of more than 3,000 meters. After arriving in [Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/), allow for acclimatization and avoid scheduling excessive physical activity on your first day. If you feel unwell, it is better to discuss changing the itinerary and seek medical advice than to insist on completing every stop.

The sun can be strong during the day, while shade and evenings may feel cool. Bring a warm layer, a hat, water, and ultraviolet protection. Comfortable shoes are suitable for walking around the site.

Opening hours, admission requirements, and demonstration formats can change. Before including the visit in a particular day's itinerary, agree on the timing and confirm that the relevant workshops will be welcoming guests.

## Awanakancha on Ada Tours Journeys

Our [“15-Day Tour of Brazil, Argentina, Chile, and Peru”](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-peru-15-days/) includes Awanakancha in the Peruvian section of a longer journey, alongside Pisac, Moray, Chinchero, and Ollantaytambo. The craft stop provides a living cultural counterpart to the archaeological sites of the Andes.

Other itineraries may offer the center as **an optional excursion**. For example, the [“Enchanting Peru and Bolivia: 10 Days in the Andes”](/multi-country/tour/enchanted-peru-bolivia-10-days/) lists a trip via Pisac, Awanakancha, and Ollantaytambo among its optional services. It should not be treated as part of the base package without checking the conditions of that specific offer.

Compare not just the number of places visited, but also what happens on each day. If traditional crafts are your main interest, leave plenty of time at the center; if archaeology matters more, you can organize your stops differently. Explore our [Peru tours](/peru/tour/) and [cultural and historical journeys in Peru](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/peru/) to help you decide.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Awanakancha

### Is Awanakancha a Zoo or a Museum?

It is a cultural and textile center with Andean camelids and craft demonstrations. Think of it as a place to discover the animals, their fibers, and the living tradition of weaving together.

### What Is the Difference Between a Llama and an Alpaca?

Llamas were traditionally used as pack animals, while alpacas are bred largely for their fiber. They are distinct domesticated camelid species with different builds and traditional uses.

### Can You See Vicuñas and Guanacos?

Both species appear in descriptions of the center, but it is best to confirm which animals will be there shortly before visiting. Wild species require particular care and handling.

### Do You Have to Buy Textiles After a Weaving Demonstration?

No. The main value of a visit is learning about traditional production and its cultural context. Buying an item is entirely up to you.

## Which Tours Offer an Optional Visit to Awanakancha?

[Awanakancha](/peru/place/awanakancha/) is a center devoted to South American camelids and Andean weaving on the road from [Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/) to [Pisac](/peru/place/pisac/). Travelers can see llamas, alpacas, vicuñas, and guanacos and learn how wool is spun, colored with natural dyes, and turned into textiles with traditional patterns.

Here we have gathered itineraries **to which you can add a visit to Awanakancha**. This is an important distinction from an included excursion: the main days of your chosen tour may feature Cusco, Machu Picchu, Lake Titicaca, and Bolivia, while a stop at Awanakancha depends on whether you select an additional activity.

Usually this is not just a quick stop for a photograph, but an entire sightseeing day in the [Sacred Valley of the Incas](/peru/place/sacred-valley-of-the-incas/) with several places to visit.

|---|---|
| Peru and Bolivia in 10 days | An additional day exploring the Sacred Valley |
| Peru, Bolivia, and Uyuni in 12 days | Available by choice alongside the main itinerary |
| Peru and Bolivia in 15 days | An optional stop on an extended journey |

On the [10-day “Enchanting Peru and Bolivia” tour](/multi-country/tour/enchanted-peru-bolivia-10-days/), the main itinerary links Peru's historic areas with Lake Titicaca and Bolivia. You can book an additional Sacred Valley excursion, taking in Pisac, Awanakancha, and Ollantaytambo. The center adds living craft traditions to a journey otherwise rich in archaeological sites and mountain scenery.

The [12-day “Peru and Bolivia with the Uyuni Salt Flats” itinerary](/multi-country/tour/peru-bolivia-uyuni-12-days/) has a broader focus: beyond Peru's cities, travelers venture into Bolivia's high-altitude landscapes. Awanakancha is available on a separate optional Sacred Valley program; its appearance in a list of places does not make it part of the mandatory days.

On the [15-day “Peru and Bolivia: Uyuni and Altiplano Lakes” trip](/multi-country/tour/peru-bolivia-uyuni-lakes-15-days/), the optional outing adds an introduction to Andean craft traditions to an extended journey. It needs to fit around the main itinerary and any other excursions you may wish to take.

**All three options require you to select the excursion separately**, even when Awanakancha appears in the tour's complete geographical list.

## What Is Included in a Sacred Valley Excursion Day?

Our optional programs combine [Pisac](/peru/place/pisac/), [Awanakancha](/peru/place/awanakancha/), and [Ollantaytambo](/peru/place/ollantaytambo/). Each offers a different experience.

In Pisac, visitors discover the local craft market and items made from ceramics, wool, silver, and leather. At Awanakancha, the focus is on South American camelids and how textiles are produced. Ollantaytambo reveals an archaeological complex, stone terraces, and ancient fortifications.

It is a full sightseeing day, best considered a complete addition to your itinerary. The program differs from a stand-alone visit to the weaving center: the entire valley route is arranged and paid for. We offer it as an optional excursion with lunch. Conditions applying to other excursions do not automatically apply to this one.

## How Is Awanakancha Different from Archaeological Sites?

Peru is often associated with Inca ruins. Awanakancha reveals another side of the region: living crafts. Watching the animals comes with an explanation of their fibers and how these are processed. Local artisans practice spinning, natural dyeing, and hand weaving, preserving techniques passed down in Andean communities.

Peru's official tourism portal describes the center as a place to discover traditional textiles and camelids. Compared with [Ollantaytambo](/peru/place/ollantaytambo/), where architecture is the main attraction, Awanakancha shows how materials and crafts figure in everyday culture.

It is a good place to ask specific questions about the different animal species and traditional dyes. The demonstrations available depend on the program and how the visit is arranged, however; do not expect a personal workshop unless one has been explicitly confirmed.

## What to Consider When Adding This Excursion

Awanakancha is in a high-altitude area near Cusco. Peru's official tourism portal gives an elevation of approximately 3,500 meters. Even without strenuous activity, a relaxed pace, water, sun protection, and warm clothing are sensible in the changeable mountain weather.

A full day in the Sacred Valley must be coordinated with the dates and conditions of the main tour. Where the itinerary includes travel to Bolivia, Machu Picchu, and other fixed excursions, the actual sequence of days determines whether there is time for an additional outing. An optional excursion cannot be promised at the same time as another scheduled trip if their hours overlap.

Journeys that include Awanakancha as a mandatory stop belong to a different selection. Here you will find **tours on which it can be added**. For more options, see our [Peru tours](/peru/tour/) and [the country's cultural and historical itineraries](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/peru/).

## Frequently Asked Questions About Tours with Awanakancha

### Is Awanakancha Included in the Base Price of These Tours?

In this selection, the visit forms part of an optional Sacred Valley excursion. Its price and inclusions must be considered separately from the main program.

### Can I Visit Only Awanakancha, Without Pisac and Ollantaytambo?

The center is a destination in its own right, but our optional programs include it in a full day with Pisac and Ollantaytambo. A different arrangement would need to be agreed separately.

### Which Is More Interesting Here: the Animals or the Weaving?

Both matter. Visitors meet llamas, alpacas, and other camelids and learn about Andean spinning, dyeing, and textiles. It is an appealing choice for anyone who enjoys cultural visits featuring working crafts.

### Do I Need Athletic Training for This Excursion?

No demanding hike is included. Nevertheless, the day takes place in the highlands of Peru, so consider your health, the elevation, and the amount of travel around the valley.

## Tours Through Awanakancha: How to Choose Your Journey

[Awanakancha](/peru/place/awanakancha/) is on the road from [Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/) to the [Sacred Valley of the Incas](/peru/place/sacred-valley-of-the-incas/). Visitors can observe South American camelids and learn how wool is made into fabric, from spinning and dyeing to working at the loom. The stop complements archaeological sites with a living craft tradition.

We offer {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} that include Awanakancha on their main itinerary. **In both cases, the center forms part of a sightseeing day, rather than a separate multi-day trip devoted to Awanakancha.** Comparing the journeys by the name “Awanakancha” alone would therefore be misleading: one centers on a New Year's holiday with Brazil, while the other takes you through four South American countries.

If your primary interest is the center itself, start with our [guide to Awanakancha](/peru/place/awanakancha/). Here we explain how it fits into the wider journeys.

## Two Itineraries That Visit Awanakancha

| Itinerary | What Kind of Journey It Offers |
|---|---|
| [New Year in Brazil and Peru](/multi-country/tour/brazil-peru-new-year/) | A festive Rio experience and an extensive introduction to Peru |
| [Brazil, Argentina, Chile, and Peru in 15 Days](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-peru-15-days/) | Four countries, ending with the Peruvian highlights |

### New Year in Rio Followed by a Journey Through Peru

The [Brazil + Peru New Year's itinerary](/multi-country/tour/brazil-peru-new-year/) begins with celebrations in Rio de Janeiro and continues in Peru through [Lima](/peru/place/lima/), Cusco, the Sacred Valley, [Machu Picchu](/peru/place/machu-picchu/), [Lake Titicaca](/peru/place/puno-and-lake-titicaca/), [Paracas](/peru/place/paracas/), and the area of the [Nazca Lines](/peru/place/nazca-lines-and-ballestas-islands/).

Awanakancha appears on the day when travelers fly from Lima to Cusco and drive into the Sacred Valley. The itinerary includes a stop to see Andean animals before heading to the market in [Pisac](/peru/place/pisac/). Here the center marks a transition from cities and airports to Andean scenery and local life.

**This route suits travelers who want to combine a New Year's celebration by the ocean with an extended journey through Peru.** Confirm the specific departure dates against the current offer: the presence of a festive itinerary in the catalog does not guarantee availability for every future New Year.

### Four Countries, with the Sacred Valley at the End

The [15-day Brazil–Argentina–Chile–Peru tour](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-peru-15-days/) starts in Rio de Janeiro, passes through Iguazu Falls, Buenos Aires, and Santiago de Chile, and concludes with Peru's attractions.

Awanakancha is included in the Sacred Valley day alongside Pisac and [Moray](/peru/place/moray/). Travelers see llamas and alpacas and learn about dyeing wool. The same trip includes Inca archaeological sites followed by Machu Picchu. Here the craft stop offers a glimpse of contemporary regional life after visits to major cities and natural landmarks across several countries.

**This option is for those who want to discover several countries in a single trip.** It involves more changes of setting than a Peru-focused itinerary, so anyone keen to spend time learning about local crafts should check how long the stop will last.

## What to See Near Awanakancha

The center combines well with [Pisac](/peru/place/pisac/), known for its market and archaeological terraces, and [Ollantaytambo](/peru/place/ollantaytambo/), where monumental stone structures survive. [Moray](/peru/place/moray/) is famous for its unusual circular agricultural terraces. These are different experiences: one focuses on crafts and animals, the others on trade, agriculture, and Inca architecture.

We also offer a stand-alone [“Sacred Valley: Pisac, Awanakancha, and Ollantaytambo” excursion](/peru/cusco/sacred-valley-pisac-awanakancha-ollantaytambo/), featuring a full-day trip and lunch. It is useful for travelers who do not want an extensive multi-country tour. **The existence of this excursion does not mean that every stop it includes is automatically part of both tours in this selection**: each itinerary has its own stops and inclusions.

## Altitude, Travel, and the Visit Format

Awanakancha is in the highlands at around 3,500 m above sea level, on the route toward the Sacred Valley. It can be chilly even when the sun shines; warm clothing, ultraviolet protection, and water are advisable for the day. If you have just arrived from a low-altitude city, take account of how your body may respond to the elevation and plan your activity accordingly.

The length of the stop depends on the day's sightseeing schedule. You can see the animals and textile-making during one visit, but talking with artisans in depth and choosing handmade items takes more free time. Check **how much time is allocated within that day**, rather than only the total length of the 15-day or holiday trip.

The center features llamas, alpacas, vicuñas, guanacos, and the textile traditions of Andean communities. Whether animals can be fed and which demonstrations are available depend on the visit arrangements. Ticket information and opening hours are best checked closer to departure because these conditions can change.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Tours with Awanakancha

### Can I Visit Awanakancha Without Traveling Through Four Countries?

Yes. You can take a separate [Sacred Valley excursion](/peru/cusco/sacred-valley-pisac-awanakancha-ollantaytambo/) from Cusco. The current selection of tours that include Awanakancha in their main itinerary consists of multi-country journeys; the stand-alone excursion is a separate product.

### What Is More Interesting at Awanakancha: Animals or Weaving?

The two themes are connected. Llamas and alpacas introduce you to Andean animal husbandry, while textile-making shows how wool is used in crafts and traditional clothing. If traveling with children, consider the arrangements for seeing the animals; if you love culture and history, allow time for the weaving demonstrations.

### Is Awanakancha Located in Cusco Itself?

No. It is a stop on the road from Cusco toward Pisac and the Sacred Valley. That makes it convenient to visit when traveling between these areas rather than dedicating a separate day in the city to it.

### Do All Trips Featuring Awanakancha Include Machu Picchu?

Both itineraries being compared include [Machu Picchu](/peru/place/machu-picchu/), but these sites are visited at different points in their programs. Check the detailed daily schedules and the current terms of your specific tour.

### Which Itinerary Is Best If I Mainly Want to Explore Peru?

If you are particularly interested in Peru's archaeology and natural scenery, also browse our [Peru tours](/peru/tour/). Multi-country programs let you combine several destinations, but a substantial part of the trip is spent in other cities, on flights, and on the road.

## Cajamarca, Peru: Inca History, Colonial Architecture, and Thermal Waters

[Cajamarca](/peru/place/cajamarca/) sits in a mountain valley of northern [Peru](/peru/) at an elevation of approximately **2,720 meters**. Visitors come for Andean history, Spanish colonial architecture, crafts, and the thermal springs of Baños del Inca. The city deserves more than a brief stop in transit: its monuments span several periods, and exploring the surrounding area takes time.

Cajamarca has particular significance in the history of the conquest of the Inca Empire. In 1532, the Inca ruler Atahualpa met a force led by Francisco Pizarro here, and the encounter ended with Atahualpa's capture. It was one of the defining events of South America's early colonial history.

## Plaza de Armas and the Historic Center

The central Plaza de Armas is a natural place to begin. Around it stand stone-faced buildings, the cathedral, and historic streets. The urban architecture combines Andean traditions with Baroque forms from the colonial period.

Another important stop is **Cuarto del Rescate**, the Ransom Room. The building is associated with the account of the gold and silver that Atahualpa promised the Spaniards in exchange for his freedom. The episode is best understood in the broader context of the conquest rather than reduced to a brief legend about treasure.

For a deeper introduction to local culture, visit museums and churches in the historic center. Check admission times and access before going, since active places of worship and museums may operate on different schedules.

## Baños del Inca: Hot Springs

Not far from Cajamarca lie **Baños del Inca**, thermal springs known in the region long before modern resort services existed. Hot water rises naturally from underground and is used in equipped pools and private bathing rooms, where the temperature is regulated.

This is a pleasant addition to a cultural sightseeing day. It is important, however, to distinguish between seeing a natural spring, purchasing access to a bathing facility, and booking a complete spa program. These involve different services and amounts of time.

Travelers wishing to combine history and relaxation may enjoy [spa and wellness itineraries](/interests/spa/). Being near hot springs does not mean that every Cajamarca tour includes bathing.

## Archaeology Nearby: Cumbemayo and Ventanillas

Several important sites lie beyond Cajamarca's central square. **Cumbemayo** is known for its ancient water channels and rock formations; visiting requires a separate outing rather than a short walk from the cathedral.

Another form of archaeological heritage found in the region consists of rock-cut niches and burial structures. Their names, access arrangements, and suitability for visits depend on the specific site. A city tour should not be confused with an excursion to every archaeological location nearby.

When choosing your route, decide what matters most: Inca history in the city center, ancient engineering, or a relaxing visit to hot springs. Combining all these experiences will require several separate outings.

## Weather and Altitude

At approximately 2,700 meters, the daytime sun can be intense, while evenings are noticeably cooler. In mountain valleys, the rainy season generally has a greater effect on walks and road conditions than on short museum visits. Sturdy footwear, water, warm clothing, and sun protection will be useful for walking tours.

Those arriving from lowland areas should consider their individual response to altitude and avoid the most strenuous activities on day one. Cajamarca may feel easier than the highest routes in southern Peru, but normal precautions still apply.

In our [Peru tour catalog](/peru/tour/), compare the actual itineraries and how many days are allocated to Cajamarca: a city appearing in a tour's geographical list does not guarantee a visit to every attraction mentioned here.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Cajamarca

### How Much Time Should I Allow for Cajamarca?

One full day may be enough for the main historic sites in the city center. If you also want to see Cumbemayo, Baños del Inca, and other nearby places, it is more convenient to allow additional time.

### Can You Bathe Directly in a Hot Spring?

Visitor facilities use specially equipped bathing rooms and pools. Confirm the current rules, water temperature, and any health-related restrictions with the specific facility.

### Is Cajamarca Associated Only with the Incas?

No. The region's history goes back much further than the Inca period, and the city's appearance also reflects its colonial heritage. Archaeological and historical visits therefore complement one another.

## Caral: Exploring One of the Oldest Cities in the Americas

**The Sacred City of Caral-Supe stands on a dry terrace above the green Supe River valley in [Peru](/peru/).** The archaeological complex is renowned for its monumental structures, plazas, and sophisticated layout. From the higher ground, you can see the striking contrast between desert slopes and the irrigated river valley.

UNESCO describes Caral as **one of the oldest centers of civilization in the Americas**, dating to approximately **3000–1800 BCE**. Its age is estimated at around **5,000 years**. This brings Peru's history into a different perspective: advanced settlements flourished here thousands of years before the Inca state.

## Why Caral Was Recognized by UNESCO

**In 2009**, the Sacred City of Caral-Supe was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. The protected area covers approximately **626 hectares**. The archaeological landscape encompasses large platforms, six prominent pyramidal structures, sunken circular plazas, and residential areas.

UNESCO highlights the complexity of the city's planning and social organization. Caral was one of several settlements in the ancient Supe valley, but it is particularly well preserved and offers insight into early urban and ceremonial life.

The surviving buildings were constructed from stone and earth. Unlike later Inca walls, Caral is especially striking for its broad platforms and open plazas, which define the plan of the entire complex. They testify to organized labor and shared ceremonies.

## What to See on a Tour of Caral

The most important thing for visitors is to understand how the structures relate to one another. The archaeological city is best appreciated as an interconnected system of public spaces rather than a collection of separate pyramids.

Key features of the site include:

| Feature | What It Reveals |
|---|---|
| Large platforms | Public architecture |
| Sunken circular plazas | Ceremonial spaces |
| Residential areas | Settlement organization |
| Supe Valley | The city's relationship with the river |

Archaeological research has uncovered evidence of a complex social life, including early use of **quipu**, a system of knotted records. Not every artifact is displayed directly at the open-air site, however. A guide can help explain the significance of the buildings without speculation or anachronisms.

## How Caral Differs from Machu Picchu

[Machu Picchu](/peru/place/machu-picchu/) dates to the Inca period of the 15th century, while Caral originated **several thousand years earlier**. The architecture, surrounding landscape, and historical context of the two sites are entirely different.

For archaeology enthusiasts, Caral offers a view of an early civilization on the Andean coast. It also demonstrates that Peru's historical heritage extends far beyond the Inca state. A visit here is not interchangeable with sightseeing in Cusco: each destination represents a different era and its own monuments.

## Getting There and Preparing for Your Visit

Caral is in the Lima region, in the Supe valley on the central coast. Reaching the archaeological area requires a road transfer from [Lima](/peru/place/lima/) or towns nearer the valley; the journey time depends on the route and road conditions.

The complex stands in open, dry terrain. Bring closed-toe shoes, water, a hat, and sun protection. The archaeological site's management regulates visitor routes, guided access, and opening hours; staying on designated paths helps prevent damage to the structures.

Allow several hours to explore the ruins, in addition to travel time. If Caral is the main goal of the day, avoid adding too many distant stops.

## Caral on Ada Tours Journeys

Our [“Discover Enchanting Peru + Iquitos”](/peru/tour/peru-iquitos-discovery/) itinerary offers Caral as **a separate optional trip**, rather than an automatically included part of every day. This distinction matters when planning your budget and time: decide in advance how an archaeological excursion fits into the main schedule.

When choosing a trip to Peru, consider which periods interest you most: early coastal civilizations, Moche and Chimú culture in the north, or Inca sites in the Andes. Combining these regions requires allowance for long transfers.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Caral

### How Old Is the Ancient City of Caral?

The archaeological complex is approximately **5,000 years old**. It originated long before the Inca state.

### Is Caral on the UNESCO List?

Yes. The Sacred City of Caral-Supe was added to the World Heritage List **in 2009**.

### What Remains at Caral?

Monumental platforms, sunken circular plazas, remnants of residential buildings, and the intricate layout of the ancient settlement.

### Can You Combine Caral with Lima?

Yes, with a separate road excursion, but both travel time and the time needed to explore the site should be planned in advance.
